toc.title: Happiness comes from the safety state
Happiness in play, stillness, and even freeze
Is there a key to happiness?
The real question: what brings you to safety?
Build your safety, then build from there

blocks.p: What is happiness? What is not happiness? And is there a key to happiness? Let's look at happiness through the Polyvagal Theory.

Someone in my discussion group, a private group for the people in my courses, posted an article title about how healthy relationships are the key to happiness. Okay, well, yeah, sure, that's great. But we know that you kind of need a polyvagal state of safety in order to get those healthy relationships.
So I asked ChatGPT, the AI software, "What's the key to happiness?" Here's what it said:

q: Happiness is a complex and subjective concept, and what brings happiness to one person may not necessarily bring happiness to another. However, some key factors that have been found to contribute to happiness include having strong relationships with loved ones, having a sense of purpose or meaning in life, feeling a sense of control over one's life and circumstances, having a positive outlook and being able to find joy in small things, and taking care of one's physical and mental health.

blocks.p: I thought that was a pretty good explanation. I'm on board with that. Overall life satisfaction is part of happiness. Having a well-regulated and balanced range of emotions could be happiness. Achievement is a big part of it for me: for myself and for the people I work with, having some achievement and success in life is connected to happiness. But you can also have happiness through solitude, just being alone. And you can have happiness through connection with others.
What makes this different, for our purposes, is that we understand happiness as an emotion that stems from the safety state.

I don't know if happiness is a single emotion. I think happiness can be experienced in different ways. When we say we're experiencing happiness, it might really be joy or connection. It might be pride. It might be achievement, or feeling like a success. Maybe awe is an experience of happiness for us. Maybe delight or surprise. There are many feelings and experiences we'd look back on and say, "I was happy in that moment," but there was a more specific type of happiness going on. The experience of joy is different from surprise, but I think we could connect both of them to a general feeling of happiness.

So I'm describing happiness not just as a feeling, but as a placeholder word for other, more specific feelings or emotions that have positive associations. We'll each experience these emotions differently, of course.

Happiness has a certain look, too. Smiling is part of happiness, though not necessarily. If you're existing in stillness or in awe, you could look back and say, "I was happy in that moment," without having been smiling. But generally, happiness has smiling associated with it. Laughter might be in there, eye crinkles, all those safety state things. Connection with others is typically a part of it, or connection with yourself: being in the present moment and connecting with what you have going on inside of you. I think being in the present moment is a pretty big part of happiness.

blocks.h: Happiness comes from the safety state

blocks.p: All these emotions, feelings and experiences, and a whole bunch more, come primarily from being in a polyvagal state of safety and social engagement, or from having enough anchoring in your safety state to feel them.

So everything in that ChatGPT answer comes from being in the safety state. Once you're in the safety state, you can do the things it lists. Having healthy relationships is part of happiness, but I'd say it's the secondary or even tertiary result of being in a polyvagal state of safety and social engagement.

The autonomic state is the primary factor. Instead of healthy relationships being the primary factor that leads to happiness, I'm saying happiness comes from safety, and that leads to healthy relationships with others. And of course, it's self-reinforcing. But the autonomic state is the primary factor. For us polyvagal nerds, that shouldn't be a radical, revolutionary statement.

blocks.h: Happiness in play, stillness, and even freeze

blocks.p: Happiness can also come in different forms. I don't just mean the feelings I listed. I mean it can come from the primary state of safety and social engagement, but also from the mixed states of play and stillness.

I don't think happiness comes from flight, fight, shutdown or freeze when those are the dominant flavors of your system. But when you have elements of those defensive states active along with safety, there might be an experience of happiness even in a freeze state.

Freeze as a defensive state is very paralyzed and panicky, or even rageful. But if you're anchored in safety, you can access freeze by watching a horror movie, or by scaring the crap out of each other. You go into a mild, very temporary freeze as you tense up and brace for something scary to happen on screen. And you can look back and say, "That movie was terrifying, but I was happy in that moment. I was connecting with my friends as we watched it."
If you're in flight or fight but your safety state's active, then you're in play. And you're probably going to have some element of happiness when you play.

So happiness can come from being anchored enough in your safety state, even while accessing the defensive states. But I don't think you'll experience happiness if you're existing primarily in flight, fight, shutdown or freeze, in a dominant defensive state.

When I ask a lot of my therapy clients how they're doing, they say, "I'm good," or "I'm fine." They don't say they're happy. Unless they're actually doing something that anchors them in their safety state and leads to happiness, what they're saying is that they're just not feeling the emotional dysregulation.

That could come from actually anchoring in their safety state and practicing the skills we're working on in therapy, but that's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about the person who's numbing their pain through phone use or some other behavioral adaptation. Usually it's the phone, especially with the teens I work with. They feel fine or good, which doesn't really mean much beyond "I'm just not feeling the dysregulation right now." And that's typically because they're distracting themselves from that pain.

That's not happiness. Distracting yourself from your pain has a function. You can cope with life that way, and it has a temporary function, absolutely. I don't want you to stop doing that. But it doesn't involve accessing your polyvagal state of safety and connection with yourself or with others. So it's not happiness.

blocks.h: Is there a key to happiness?

blocks.p: There are so many books out there that say there is. They have it, and they want to sell it to you. I respect that. That's fine. But I'd say no, there's not. I don't think there's a key. I don't think there's a secret to happiness.

The things we usually treat as keys to happiness are a result of accessing your safety state: better relationships, forgiveness, empathy for other people, being successful, having a purpose to your life, having a positive outlook, the things in that ChatGPT answer. All of these come from having access to, and being grounded in, your polyvagal state of safety. These are not secrets. These are not keys to happiness. They're the result of being in a safety state. And I don't exactly mean literal safety in the environment, or interpersonally. I mean you're accessing your biological pathways for safety.

So we're very backwards in how we understand happiness and how to get to it. We look at what happens after we're accessing our safety state and call it the key to unlocking happiness. We look at the healthy relationships that develop after being grounded in safety and say, "The healthy relationships caused the happiness." Of course they reinforce it. But forgiveness, empathy and healthy relationships primarily come after being grounded in your safety state.

I'm not talking about having healthy co-regulation and safe relationships in childhood. I'm talking about as you get older and come out of a traumatized state: if you're doing this on your own, you first have to have some self-regulation to get to safety, which then leads to the things we associate with happiness.

Instead, we look at things in reverse order: you have to have empathy first, you have to have compassion first, and then finally you'll be able to be happy. But you can't just flick these on. You can't really just turn on empathy. You can't just turn on forgiveness or healthy relationships, or success exactly. How do we have strong relationships with loved ones in the first place? I don't think anyone ever explains how to flick that switch in order to then feel happy.

So I went ahead and asked ChatGPT for ten ways to improve relationships, to see if there was something in there we could latch onto to get better relationships, and then happiness. Here's what it said:

ol: Showing interest and actively listening to what they have to say.
Being willing to compromise and make sacrifices.
Being able to forgive and move on from conflicts.
Continuously working on the relationship through effort and commitment.

blocks.p: All ten of these seem to require some safety state activation as well. No one tells us how to have the strong relationships that get us to happiness. They say strong relationships equal happiness. Okay, but how? Even these ten examples all require some safety state activation, I think.

blocks.h: The real question: what brings you to safety?

blocks.p: So the issue is not what makes you happy, or what the key to happiness is. For our purposes, the issue becomes: what first brings you to safety, so that you can then do the things that lead to happiness? What brings you to safety so you can have the open and honest communication you need for strong relationships with loved ones, which will help you feel happy?

It's not simply how to get better relationships to feel happy. It's what brings you to safety and opens you up to connection, so you can do things like communicate in a healthy way and build stronger relationships. Or, as another example, what grounds you in safety, which then gives you a stronger anchoring in your values and healthier boundaries, so you can have more empathy, connect with people, and build stronger relationships, which then reinforce your happiness?
It comes down to what grounds your body in your safety state.

Here's my example. When I'm more dysregulated, sometimes I just feel like numbing out and playing video games. It's a distraction. It's not grounding me in my safety state. It's simply distracting myself. And that can be okay. I'm not saying don't do that. All these little behavioral adaptations we do can be abused, can be taken too far. For me, video games are purely a distraction.

The alternative, through self-regulation, is that I ground myself in my safety state by mindfully experiencing the present moment. I listen to what my body needs. Maybe it needs quiet. Maybe it needs movement. Then, when I'm grounded, I'm able to connect with my wife or play with my kids. I'm able to make dinner in happiness, even though I absolutely hate cooking. Maybe I even mindfully experience the scents and flavors of making dinner. If I just play video games, I don't get to do those things. That just distracts me and kind of numbs me out.

So I have to ground myself in safety first, and then I'm able to do the things that bring me feelings of happiness. The things are not the primary factor. The way I understand it, the safety state is the primary factor, and it allows me to do the behaviors that bring up and reinforce feelings of happiness.

Once you have more anchoring in your safety state, a stronger vagal brake, you'll be able to work on further trauma if that's what you're going for. But for our purposes here, the more you anchor yourself in your safety state, the more happiness you'll potentially be able to create.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: Build your safety, then build from there

blocks.p: So it's not about "do this behavior, do that behavior." It's about how you build the strength of your safety system:

ul: Can you identify what your safety state feels like?
Do you know which mindful practices help you feel more in your safety state?
Can you build from there into happiness?

blocks.p: Go easy on yourself, though. I don't think happiness is easily attained. I feel like I'm still working on it. There are plenty of things I'm working on that help me feel more in my safety state, more connection, more happiness even. It's not easy. Go easy on yourself.

And I'd say it's definitely possible to feel happiness even when you're living in a generally traumatized state. It's difficult. It's probably harder to access your safety state and stay there. Yes. I know. But generally, it is possible.

So don't look for the one technique or behavior that somehow triggers a feeling of happiness. Identify what helps you feel more grounded in your safety state. Experience that, and build that. Then use it as a platform to feel more happiness.
